beats.intro: Chapter six. [[sub]]Hypothesis testing turns a claim about a population into a decision, with the risk of being wrong made explicit.
beats.why: [[a]]Suppose a strategy claims an average monthly return of zero. We observe a sample mean of one point two percent. Is that just luck? [[curve]]If the true mean were zero, sample means would form a bell curve around zero, with a spread equal to the standard error, here point five. [[obs]]Where does our observation fall? [[far]]It lands far out in the tail. If luck is a poor explanation, we doubt the claim.
beats.steps: [[a]]Every test follows the same seven steps. [[s1]]State the hypotheses. [[s2]]Identify the test statistic and its distribution. [[s3]]Specify the significance level. [[s4]]State the decision rule. [[s5]]Collect the data and calculate the statistic. [[s6]]Make the statistical decision. [[s7]]Then make the economic decision: is the result large enough to matter?
beats.hypotheses: [[a]]The null hypothesis is what we assume is true unless the evidence says otherwise. The alternative is what we accept if we reject the null. [[two]]In a two-sided test, the alternative says the mean is simply different from zero. We reject in either tail. [[one]]In a one-sided test, the alternative says the mean is greater than zero. We reject only in the right tail. [[note]]The null always contains the equal sign.
beats.errors: [[a]]A test can go wrong in two ways. [[t1]]Type one error: we reject a true null. Its probability is the significance level, alpha. [[t2]]Type two error: we fail to reject a false null. Its probability is beta. [[pow]]The power of a test, one minus beta, is the chance of correctly rejecting a false null. [[trade]]For a fixed sample size, lowering alpha raises beta.
beats.critical: [[a]]The decision rule compares the test statistic with critical values. [[alpha]]With a five percent significance level in a two-sided test, five percent is split into two and a half percent per tail. [[crit]]For a large sample, the critical values are minus and plus one point nine six. [[one]]For a one-sided test, all five percent sits in one tail, and the critical value is one point six four five. [[rule]]If the statistic falls beyond a critical value, we reject the null.
beats.mean: [[a]]Test whether a fund's mean monthly return differs from zero. We have thirty-six months, a sample mean of one point two percent, and a standard deviation of three percent. [[se]]The standard error is three divided by the square root of thirty-six: point five. [[t]]The t statistic is one point two minus zero, over point five: two point four. [[crit]]With thirty-five degrees of freedom, the five percent two-sided critical value is two point oh three. [[dec]]Two point four is beyond two point oh three, so we reject the null. [[eco]]But is one point two percent a month economically meaningful after costs and risk? That is the economic decision.
beats.q2: Quick check. Compute the test statistic.
beats.pvalue: [[a]]The p-value is the smallest significance level at which we could reject the null. [[tail]]It is the probability, if the null is true, of a statistic at least as extreme as ours. For our t of two point four, the two-sided p-value is about point oh two two. [[rule]]If the p-value is smaller than alpha, we reject. Point oh two two is below point oh five, so we reject. [[one]]At one percent, we would not. [[mult]]Beware of running many tests. With twenty tests at five percent, one false positive is expected by chance alone.
beats.other: [[a]]Different questions use different test statistics. [[t]]A single mean uses the t statistic we just computed. [[diff]]To compare two means, use a t test for independent samples, or a paired test when observations are matched. [[chi]]To test whether one variance equals a value, use chi-square: n minus one, times the sample variance, over the hypothesized variance. [[f]]To compare two variances, use the F statistic: the ratio of the two sample variances.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Hypothesis testing follows seven steps, from stating the null and alternative to the economic decision. [[w2]]Type one error rejects a true null; type two fails to reject a false one. Power is one minus beta. [[w3]]Reject when the statistic passes a critical value, or when the p-value is below alpha. [[w4]]Use t for means, chi-square for one variance, and F for two variances. [[end]]Now try the chapter practice.
beats.finish: Well done. That is the end of chapter six, and of this volume.
